pages.title: Thomas Hobbes: Introduction and Perspective as Thinker
pages.summary: Thomas Hobbes was an English political philosopher who witnessed the Puritan Revolution, civil war, and anarchy, making order and self-preservation central to his philosophy. He is characterized as a materialist, utilitarian, individualist, absolutist, and social contract thinker who introduced theories of the right to life and sovereignty.

pages.title: Hobbes's Methodology and Social Contract Tradition
pages.summary: Hobbes was the first to apply a scientific method to political science and belonged to the social contract tradition reflecting the historical shift from feudalism to capitalism. In contrast to ancient organic and medieval divine views, the modern mechanistic view treats the state as a human creation where man is prior to the state.

pages.title: Social Contract Steps and Hobbes's Scientific Methodology
pages.summary: Social contract thinkers analyze human nature, the state of nature, the contract, and its outcomes to demonstrate that the state arises from human will. Influenced by Galileo's resolutive-compositive method and Descartes, Hobbes formulated his political theory using scientific principles of elemental parts and matter in motion.

pages.title: Hobbes: Scientific Method, Mind, and Human Nature
pages.summary: Hobbes applied geometry, physics, psychology, and the resolutive-compositive method to explain political phenomena through human behavior and the motion of particles in the mind. He argued that actions are driven by material emotions of inclination and aversion, making individuals naturally utilitarian, equal, and guided by passions.

pages.title: Hobbes on Human Nature and Power Pursuit
pages.summary: Hobbes posits that human life is a perpetual search for power after power until death to ensure ongoing pleasure amid limited resources and endless appetites. Because people cannot comprehend others' thoughts and power is the sole means to pleasure, intense competition creates mutual insecurity and discomfort.

pages.title: Hobbes: State of Nature and Contract Reasons
pages.summary: In the state of nature, continuous competition for power produces a security dilemma and a war of all against all where human life is nasty, poor, brutish, and short. Utilitarian individuals enter into a social contract primarily to preserve their lives, as death terminates all pleasure.

pages.title: Hobbes: Fear, Self-Preservation, and Contract Features
pages.summary: Hobbes identified fear—especially the fear of death—as the psychological basis of political obligation, driving individuals to establish the state for self-preservation. In the contract, all people mutually agree to transfer their natural rights to the commonwealth on the condition that everyone else does the same.

pages.title: Hobbes: Contract Outcomes and State Authority Limitations
pages.summary: The contract establishes a sovereign, absolute police state as a third-party guarantor to ensure life security in exchange for individual liberty. The state's power is limited only by the right to self-preservation, granting individuals the right to resist if the state fails to protect or arbitrarily takes life.

pages.title: Hobbes: Theory and Characteristics of State Sovereignty
pages.summary: Sovereignty is the supreme, permanent, and indivisible power of the state, making sovereign law supreme over religious authorities and customs. The state retains police power to punish disobedience and prevent society from degenerating back into anarchy.

pages.title: Origin of Sovereignty and the Nation-State
pages.summary: The rise of capitalism and the bourgeoisie led to the emergence of centralized nation-states defined by territory, population, government, and sovereignty with a monopoly on force. Sovereignty embodies supreme internal power over citizens and external independence from foreign authorities like the Roman Church.

pages.title: Hobbes's Theory of Law
pages.summary: Hobbes links sovereignty to positive law, defining law as the command of the sovereign backed by enforcement and punishment. He critiques natural law because human reason is sufficient only to satisfy desires rather than control them to maintain peace.

pages.title: Hobbes: Theory of Rights and Self-Preservation
pages.summary: Hobbes argues that true law requires state enforcement, viewing international law as weak and akin to the state of nature where might was right. Under his theory of legal rights, rights are granted by the state, with the transfer of the supreme right to life being conditional.

pages.title: Hobbes: Right to Self-Preservation and Liberty
pages.summary: The state cannot arbitrarily deprive an individual of self-preservation except through procedure established by law. Hobbes frames negative liberty as existing where the law is silent, contrasting it with the anarchy of the state of nature which led utilitarian individuals to surrender rights to the state.

pages.title: Hobbes: Theory of Liberty and State Authority
pages.summary: Hobbes defines liberty as the absence of external impediments to motion rather than internal capacity, preferring order and security over liberty. Under an absolute state, individuals possess freedom only where the state chooses not to make laws.

pages.title: Hobbes: Modern Sovereignty and Methodological Individualism
pages.summary: Hobbes is assessed as the first modern thinker who provided a complete theory of sovereignty over both secular and religious spheres. He is also classified as a methodological individualist whose resolutive-compositive method demonstrated that utilitarian humans are naturally self-centered.

pages.title: Hobbes: Normative Individualism, Absolutism, and Leviathan
pages.summary: Hobbes reconciles individualism and absolutism by showing that an absolute state is necessary to protect individuals, granting them the right to self-preservation and resistance against arbitrary deprivation of life. His controversial masterpiece Leviathan faced harsh condemnation and was banned and burned by church and university authorities.

pages.title: Significance and Defense of Hobbes's Leviathan
pages.summary: The notes defend Leviathan against critics, explaining that Hobbes sought to establish the sovereignty of the modern state rather than provide an anthropological history. Leviathan is praised as essential for understanding modern state principles, earning recognition as a masterpiece in political philosophy and English literature.

flashcards.front: How does C.B. Macpherson characterize Thomas Hobbes's sociological perspective in Leviathan?
flashcards.back: Macpherson characterizes Hobbes as a scholar of the bourgeois class. His philosophy reflects the emerging capitalist market order, which relies on contract and necessitates state-enforced security of life.

flashcards.front: What scientific methodology did Hobbes adopt from Galileo to construct his political philosophy?
flashcards.back: Hobbes adopted Galileo's resolutive-compositive method to establish a scientific study of politics. This method decomposes complex phenomena into their elemental parts to discover underlying laws and explain the whole.

flashcards.front: How does Hobbes explain human motivation and emotions through his materialist psychology?
flashcards.back: Hobbes argues that the human mind consists of particles in motion that react to external stimuli through two basic emotions: inclination and aversion. This proves man is naturally utilitarian and individualistic, incapable of feeling another person's pleasure or pain.

flashcards.front: Why does Hobbes characterize life in the hypothetical state of nature as 'nasty, poor, brutish, and short'?
flashcards.back: Because man possesses an endless appetite for power to secure future pleasure, acquiring power creates a security dilemma that makes others insecure. This produces a state of war of all against all where no industry, navigation, or culture can flourish.

flashcards.front: What is the philosophical and biographical significance of Hobbes's statement that 'I and fear were born together'?
flashcards.back: Biographically, Hobbes's mother gave premature birth to him out of fear of the Spanish Armada. Philosophically, Hobbes identifies fear of violent death as the core psychological motive that compels utilitarian men to institute the state.

flashcards.front: Under what condition does an individual retain the right to resist the sovereign state in Hobbes's philosophy?
flashcards.back: Individuals surrender all natural rights except the supreme right to self-preservation. If the sovereign fails to protect life or attempts to take a subject's life in an arbitrary manner, the individual retains the right to resist.

flashcards.front: Why does Hobbes assert that 'covenants without swords are nothing but words'?
flashcards.back: Hobbes belongs to the positive law tradition and contends that law must be definite and backed by enforcement. Because human reason is insufficient to control selfish passions, voluntary covenants lack binding authority without the sovereign's sword.

flashcards.front: How does Hobbes define liberty, and how does his liquid in a bottle metaphor illustrate this concept?
flashcards.back: Hobbes defines liberty strictly as the absence of external impediments to motion. In his metaphor, bottle walls act as external impediments to liquid; removing them grants freedom of motion, distinguishing external liberty from internal capacity.

flashcards.front: Why is Hobbes credited with jumping inside modernity while Jean Bodin merely stood at its gate?
flashcards.back: Bodin introduced sovereignty as supreme power over citizens but remained bound to medieval thinking by subordinating the secular state to church supremacy in religion. Hobbes completed modern sovereignty by placing the church and religious law entirely under state command.

flashcards.front: Why does George Sabine designate Thomas Hobbes as the 'greatest of all individualists'?
flashcards.back: Hobbes bases his entire political theory on the self-interested nature of man, treating individualism as an objective natural fact rather than a sin. His absolute state is not an end in itself but merely a functional instrument created to protect the individual.

answers.question: Examine the apparent paradox between Hobbes's absolutism and his individualism. Is it correct to describe him as the greatest of all individualists? Comment.
answers.intro: Thomas Hobbes is often considered both the greatest absolutist and greatest individualist. As Sabine observed, Hobbes's political philosophy does not subordinate the individual to the state; rather, it constructs an absolute sovereign solely to preserve self-interested individuals.
body: Employing Galileo's resolutive-compositive method, Hobbes constructs methodological individualism, demonstrating that atomic human motions produce utilitarian appetite and aversion, rendering individuals fundamentally incapable of understanding the pleasures or pains of fellow citizens.

Hobbes establishes normative individualism by asserting that self-interest is an objective natural fact rather than moral sin, prompting C.B. Macpherson to designate Hobbes as the authentic theorist of the emerging bourgeois market society.

Absolutism and individualism are fully reconciled because the sovereign state is a purely mechanistic creation; individuals institute the Leviathan through social contract exclusively to escape the violent state of nature and secure personal self-preservation.

Hobbes preserves the inviolable right to life, permitting subjects to resist the sovereign if arbitrarily threatened, validating George Sabine's assertion that Hobbesian absolute power is merely an operational tool serving radical individualism.

Countering C.E. Vaughan's critique of Leviathan as fruitless, Karl Marx acknowledged Hobbes as an intellectual father because his political architecture treats individual material existence and utility as the supreme foundation of modern governance.
answers.conclusion: Hobbes's absolutism is therefore the outer shell protecting an individualistic core. By anchoring state authority on human utility and the preservation of life, Hobbes laid the secular foundations of modern constitutionalism and individual rights.

answers.question: Critically evaluate Hobbes's assertion that 'covenants without swords are nothing but words'. How does his theory of sovereignty establish the modern positive law tradition?
answers.topic: Hobbes's Theory of Law and Sovereignty
answers.intro: In Leviathan, Thomas Hobbes revolutionized political jurisprudence by defining law as the command of the sovereign. Rejecting medieval natural law, he argued that covenants lack binding force without a coercive sovereign sword to guarantee social peace.
body: Hobbes rejects natural law as mere 'articles of peace' or counsels of prudence because human passions inevitably overpower reason; without sovereign positive enforcement, private covenants dissolve into anarchic civil conflict.

Founding the positive law tradition, Hobbes insists authentic law must be definite and enforceable, replacing medieval customary traditions with the sovereign state's absolute monopoly over the use of punitive physical force.

While Jean Bodin remained trapped at modernity's gate by preserving ecclesiastical supremacy, Hobbes jumped into modernity by establishing indivisible sovereignty that explicitly subordinated the church and canon laws to civil authority.

Hobbes demonstrates the weakness of international law, which lacks an overarching sword of enforcement, thereby leaving global politics lingering in an anarchic state of nature where power remains both means and end.

As C.B. Macpherson observed, this definitive legal sovereign served the rising bourgeois class, replacing feudal customary confusion with clear statutory contracts indispensable for commercial capitalist expansion and state stability.
answers.conclusion: Hobbesian sovereignty decisively shifted jurisprudence from divine natural law to positive state command. By demonstrating that laws require enforcement to secure peace, Hobbes provided the foundational framework for modern sovereign nation-states.
